Chapter 16

Biopolymer-based hydrogels and their composites for enhanced adsorptive removal of dyes: recent perspectives

Debolina Ghosh[1](#_bookmark0) and Gopal Das[1](#_bookmark0),[2](#_bookmark0)

_1Centre for Environment, Indian Institute of Technology Guwahati, Guwahati, Assam, India, 2Department of Chemistry, Indian Institute of Technology Guwahati, Guwahati, Assam, India_

# Introduction

The exponential growth in human population has imposed a severe increasing demand for Earth’s limited clean water sup-ply. In the current situation, where water is being continuously squandered for industrial and agricultural demands, safe-guarding our natural water resources must be our primary concern ([Katheresan, Kansedo, & Lau, 2018; Pavithra, S.K.,](#_bookmark37) [Jaikumar, & S.R., 2019; Roy & Saha, 2020](#_bookmark37)). With the enormous growth of textile industries globally, large volumes of water are consumed during the manufacture of textile products, particularly by dyeing and printing operations ([Dawood &](#_bookmark18) [Sen, 2014; Zhou, Lu, Zhou, & Liu, 2019](#_bookmark18)). A textile facility with a daily manufacturing capacity of 8000 kg consumes approximately 1.6 million liters of fresh water per day ([Behera, Nayak, Banerjee, Chakrabortty, & Tripathy, 2021; Gupta](#_bookmark13) [& Suhas, 2009; Vishnu, Dhandapani, Authilingam, & Sivakumar, 2022](#_bookmark13)). As a result of this, the effluents released com-prise organic chemicals, surfactants, heavy metals, emerging contaminants, synthetic dyes, etc. The majority of these efflu-ents emitted into water bodies are poisonous and hazardous, creating negative human and ecological health effects that require prompt and effective intervention. The disposal of unwanted materials and chemicals (e.g., heavy metals, emerging contaminants, organic materials, and synthetic dyes) into the water bodies without adequate treatment becomes harmful to plants, animals, microorganisms, and human beings. The uncontrolled discharge of dyes in wastewater severely threatens plant and aquatic life ([Islam et al., 2021; Sachan, Ghosh, & Das, 2023; Sardar, Manna, Maharana, & Sen, 2020](#_bookmark33)). These synthetic dyes comprise very stable heterocyclic and aromatic groups that are incredibly resistant to degradation and are therefore recalcitrant. The high chemical oxygen demand, high color, and poor biochemical degradability of dyes, as well as the carcinogenic, teratogenic, and nonbiodegradable characteristics, have drawn the attention of researchers who are always searching for treatment methods for dye remediation from wastewater ([Sharma, 2015; Teo et al., 2022](#_bookmark65)).

In the last three decades, several physical, chemical, and biological methods have emerged such as flocculation, oxida-tion, solvent extraction process, precipitation, degradation, ion exchange, membrane filtration, coagulation, electrochemis-try, biodegradation, and phytoremediation ([Dawood & Sen, 2014; Kandisa and Saibaba KV, 2016; Pavithra et al., 2019;](#_bookmark18) [Ramakrishna and Viraraghavan, 1997; Roy and Saha, 2020; Katheresan et al., 2018](#_bookmark18)). Each of these operational approaches has advantages, but their limitations outweigh their advantages due to the expense and complexity of the operation pro-cess. However, among them owing to its simplicity, great performance, recyclability, and low cost, the adsorption tech-nique has been widely utilized to remove organic dye contaminants from wastewater ([Tang, Wang, Yin, & Lo, 2010;](#_bookmark69) [Wang et al., 2021](#_bookmark69)). The use of low-cost adsorbents with rapid adsorption rates, higher efficiency, and optimum reusability features is the main focal point among researchers. In this aspect, polymers and more specifically biopolymers have attained great attention ([Holkar, Jadhav, Pinjari, Mahamuni, & Pandit, 2016; Yang et al., 2022](#_bookmark31)).

Regarding wastewater treatment, hydrogels have exhibited superior performance in the adsorptive removal of sev-eral inorganic and organic pollutants. A hydrogel is a tridimensional polymeric structure with flexibility, biocompatibil-ity, biodegradability, and swelling and collapsing properties. The ability to swell in the dispersion medium arises from the hydrophilic functional groups located in the polymeric backbone. In contrast, its resistance to dissolution occurs

from the crosslinking between its polymeric network chains ([Khan and Lo, 2016; Shalla, Bhat, & Yaseen, 2018](#_bookmark38)). Hydrophilic polymers refer to polymeric networks that comprise polar functional groups such as hydroxyl (—OH), car-boxyl (—COOH), and amino (—NH2) groups, which make them easily soluble and swelled up by water and other aque-ous pollutants that adhere not only to the hydrogel surface but also within the interconnected polymeric matrices ([Ahmadian and Jaymand, 2023; Pereira, Rodrigues, Paulino, Martins, & Fajardo, 2021](#_bookmark9)). In many ways, hydrogels are comparable to ion-exchange resins; for example, they are polymeric materials that primarily remove aqueous contami-nants through electrostatic interactions. However, unlike resins, which have hard structures, hydrogels have flexible structures and can absorb far more water than resins ([Tang et al., 2010; Van Tran, Park, & Lee, 2018](#_bookmark69)). A striking advantage in the case of these hydrogels is that they can be prepared from either natural, synthetic or a combination of both sources. Furthermore, the modification of hydrogels through the entrapment of various fillers, such as metals, nanoparticles, clays, MOFs, and organic fillers, can result in a variety of hydrogel-based composites with improved properties in terms of adsorption capacity, thermal and chemical stability, mechanical robustness, etc. ([Ghosh, De,](#_bookmark24) [Deka, & Das, 2024; Kabiri, Omidian, Zohuriaan-Mehr, & Doroudiani, 2011](#_bookmark24)). This chapter gives a detailed overview of the application of hydrogels or biopolymer hydrogels on dye removal.

# Dye—a brief overview and its removal

Numerous industries and company markets that procure, produce as well as utilize dyes, discharge dye effluents into the environment, which are detrimental to both living creatures and the environment. As a result, both citizens and environmentalists are becoming increasingly concerned about the presence of dye effluent in environmental water bod-ies. These synthetic dyes play a vital role in leather, tanning, paper, and pulp as well as textile industries. However, once the work is completed, the remaining dyes are straight away discarded into the water bodies without care and treatment ([Dutta, Gupta, Srivastava, & Gupta, 2021; Katheresan et al. 2018](#_bookmark20)). These dye effluents comprise several haz-ardous organic chemicals, which endanger the lives of both humans and aquatic animals. The two main parts of dye molecules are the chromophores that impart color and the auxochromes, which can be added to the chromophore in addition to making the molecule soluble in water and providing increased affinity (to connect) to the fibers. Most of these chemicals are recalcitrant and very much stable to degradation and oxidation. Hence, they form a layer over the water bodies due to their low density and block the penetration of sunlight ([Bilal, Ihsanullah, Hassan Shah, Bhaskar](#_bookmark14) [Reddy, & Aminabhavi, 2022; Moradi and Sharma, 2021; Teo et al., 2022](#_bookmark14)).

## Classification of dyes

Dyes show significant structural variety and can be categorized in several ways. Dyes can be classified based on their structure, application, solubility, etc. Examples of soluble dyes are acid, basic, direct, mordant, and reactive dyes; exam-ples of insoluble dyes are azo, disperse, sulfur, and vat dyes. Among all these different types of dyes, azo dyes are the most globally produced and predominantly used dyes. A summary of the different kinds of dyes has been categorized in [Table 16.1](#_bookmark1) ([Gupta and Suhas, 2009; Katheresan et al. 2018; Patel, 2018; Pavithra et al., 2019](#_bookmark27)).

## Methods of dye removal

There is general agreement in the literature currently in publication that colored effluents need to be thoroughly treated to eliminate all dyestuff before being disposed of. Toxic dyes have been removed from wastewater and water reservoirs using a variety of physical, chemical, and biological processes developed during the past few decades. Even though a lot of dye removal techniques have been studied over the past 30 years, only a small number of them are being used by the relevant industries these days due to the bulk of the techniques’ limitations. Most of these processes are economi-cally unfeasible, require huge chemicals, produce a large number of by-products, have high energy consumption, and are not environment friendly. The techniques commonly used for dye treatment have been described in [Fig. 16.1](#_bookmark2) ([Ahmadian and Jaymand, 2023; Dutta et al., 2021; Katheresan et al. 2018; Teo et al., 2022](#_bookmark9)).

# Hydrogel—an overview

In this chapter, the principal material of interest is hydrogel, which is defined as polymeric gel networks that are signifi-cantly swollen in water or any other biological media. In other words, the word “gel_”_ was coined by 19th-century Scottish chemist Thomas Graham by clipping from gelatine. Gels are well-known soft materials that find a variety of

multipurpose applications in our daily lives ([Cornwell, Okesola, & Smith, 2013; Njuguna and Scho¨nherr, 2022; Seida](#_bookmark17) [and Tokuyama, 2022](#_bookmark17)). A gel is typically a semisolid that can range from soft and weak to hard and tough and is defined as a diluted crosslinked system consisting of a liquid component present in adequate quantity and two or more other solid-like components, which depicts no flow when observed in its steady state. This solid-like phase makes up only a

very small percentage of the overall composition of the material. A big class of these gels is called hydrogel or hydro-philic gel that is a three-dimensional network of polymers that swell up in water or a biological medium. Similarly, when the dispersion medium is an organic solvent, it is called an organogel ([Li et al., 2021; Thakur et al., 2022](#_bookmark42)).

A hydrogel is a three-dimensional polymeric structure that can expand and contract, be biocompatible and biode-gradable, and have these characteristics. The hydrophilic functional groups in the polymeric backbone provide it the capacity to swell in the dispersion medium, while the crosslinking between the polymeric network chains gives it the ability to resist dissolution. Hydrophilic polymers refer to polymeric networks that comprise polar functional groups such as hydroxyl (—OH), carboxyl (—COOH), and amino (—NH2), which readily dissolve in water and swell up. Hydrogels can be crosslinked in either a physical or reversible manner, in the form of molecular entanglements, or can be chemically crosslinked by crosslinkers using covalent interactions. Recently, there has been increasing research inter-est in the development and application of novel hydrogels in wastewater treatment. Due to their unique physical and chemical properties such as hydrophilicity, swelling properties, and response to external environmental influences, they have attained considerable attention ([Li, Liu, & Chen, 2018; Yang et al., 2022](#_bookmark43)). A detailed analysis of their classifica-tion is described below.

## Classification of hydrogels

The hydrogels can be classified based on many categories. Based on the source, broadly hydrogels can be divided into two types: natural and synthetic.

Natural hydrogels are prepared from natural sources of origin. Chitosan (CS) is a source obtained from the structural exoskeleton of crustaceans, whereas agarose and alginate are some natural polysaccharide-based polymers obtained from seaweed. Similarly, synthetic hydrogels are prepared using synthetic polymer origins that are considered to have longer service life with tailorable functionality better suited for vast applications. Polyvinyl alcohol, polyethylene gly-col, and poly-_N_\-isopropyl acrylamide are some examples of synthetic polymer sources for the development of synthetic hydrogels. Another alternative is semisynthetic hydrogels that consist of a combination of both the above classes of hydrogels ([Li et al., 2018, 2021; Thakur et al., 2022; Yang et al., 2022](#_bookmark43)).

Based on crosslinking, physical crosslinking comprises physical-polymer chain entanglements or physical associations such as ionic interactions, hydrophobic interactions, or hydrogen bonding that result in physical, transient networks. Crystallization, stereo-complex interactions, and protein-based interactions are some other methods of physically crosslinked hydrogels. The freezing—thawing process of crystallization is a common method of preparation of physically tough and elas-tic hydrogels. In the chemical crosslinking method of hydrogel preparation, a crosslinker is added to the polymeric solution, and the polymer having appropriate functionality results in the formation of permanent crosslinking networks within the hydrogel matrix. Chemically crosslinked hydrogels are formed by chain growth addition and condensation polymerization reactions. Different crosslinking agents can be used to achieve different adjustable properties such as higher mechanical strength and stability owing to the chemical bonds. Hydrogels also exhibit different types of behavior based on their cross-linking ratio. The higher the crosslinker ratio, the more tough and stronger hydrogels are formed with lesser swelling ability, whereas the lower the crosslinker ratio results, in soft hydrogels with higher swelling ability ([Bustamante-Torres et al., 2021;](#_bookmark15) [Coviello et al., 2013; Gulrez, Al-Assaf, & O, 2011](#_bookmark15)).

Based on network electrical charge, hydrogels are categorized mainly based on the electrical charge located on the net-work chains. They can be neutral or nonionic. When neutral polysaccharides covalently crosslink with neutral polysacchar-ides and/or neutral monomeric units such as acrylamide, _N_\-vinyl pyrrolidone, and hydroxyalkyl methacrylate to form three-dimensional polymeric networks, the network is called a neutral hydrogel. These gels are irreversible and can absorb water without dissolution. These hydrogels demonstrate temperature-sensitive swelling—deswelling behavior.

Ionic hydrogels, on the other hand, are broadly of two types: cationic and anionic. When ionic polymers are cova-lently crosslinked with each other to form a 3-D polymeric network, these are known as ionic hydrogels. CS is a natu-rally available cationic polysaccharide obtained from the partial alkaline deacetylation of chitin. Polysaccharides extracted from seaweeds (alginate, agar, and carrageenan) and plant cell walls (pectin) and exudates (gum arabic) are anionic and have been predominantly used in the food industry as gelling agents ([Garg, Garg, & Vishwavidyalaya,](#_bookmark23) [2016; Maitra and Shukla, 2014; Peppas and Hoffman, 2020; Thakur, Thakur, & Arotiba, 2018](#_bookmark23)).

## Synthesis routes for the preparation of hydrogels

The main synthesis of hydrogels involves physical, chemical, and hybrid bonding. The bonding is formed via different routes, such as solution casting, solution mixing, bulk polymerization, free radical mechanism, radiation method, and

interpenetrating network formation. To achieve proper hydrogels, it is necessary to undergo several modifications on the polymer subjected to several tailor-made specifications so that it can be better suited for several applications. One method to modify polymer properties is blending, which is a method of physical mixing of two polymers to achieve the desired hydrogel. Another known method is grafting, where the monomers are covalently bonded to the polymeric backbone. The chemical crosslinking method includes covalent bonding of the monomer units into the polymeric chain, by using several crosslinking agents. Curing is another process, where the polymerization of the oligomeric mixture forms a coating on the surface, adhered by physical forces ([Ahmed, 2015; Liu, Wang, Chen, & Cheng, 2022; Sahu,](#_bookmark10) [Gupta, & Nautiyal, 2020; Varaprasad, Raghavendra, Jayaramudu, Yallapu, & Sadiku, 2017](#_bookmark10)).

## Characterization methods for hydrogel

Numerous characterization techniques are already available that focus on hydrogel properties in either the macro- or micro-scale (morphology and topology) and are based on qualitative or quantitative evaluation. The proper characterization is required to design hydrogels with optimum performance, and a strong, robust structural network, making them an ideal can-didate for dye adsorption. Physicochemical characterization of the hydrogel includes swelling measurement, sol—gel analy-sis, gel content, ultraviolet—visible (UV) spectroscopy, and solubility tests. Hydrogel structural insights can be explored using fourier-transform infrared (FTIR), nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR, X-ray diffraction (XRD), Raman spectroscopies, etc. Thermal transition and stability studies of the hydrogel can be studied by thermogravimetric analysis (TGA), differential scanning calorimetry (DSC), and differential thermal analysis (DTA) spectroscopy. Deformation heating rates and conductiv-ity studies can be understood using these techniques. Mass spectroscopy can be used to identify unknown compounds within the gel network, whereas dynamic light scattering (DLS) can give an account of the particle size as well as the dispersion ability of the hydrogels. Dynamic mechanical studies such as rheological properties as well as tensile strength and compres-sive strength can be analyzed using rheometer and universal testing machine (UTM) instruments, respectively. Morphological and microscopic characterization is essential for comprehending the surface morphology, topology, and over-all shape and surface properties of the hydrogel. This can be done using scanning and transimission electron microscopy (SEM, TEM), and atomic force microscopy (AFM) techniques ([Fig. 16.2](#_bookmark3)). Not only this, but also the porosity of the hydro-gel can be visualized using this microscopic characterization method. These tools play an important role in designing and production of good-quality hydrogels that can be finetuned for a variety of multipurpose applications ([Ahmed, 2015; Ghosh,](#_bookmark10) [Basak, Deka, & Das, 2022; Ghosh, Basak, Deka, & Das, 2023; Seera, Kundu, Gami, Naik, & Banerjee, 2021](#_bookmark10)).

# Biopolymer hydrogels for dye removal

Hydrogels, particularly biopolymer based in origin, have been studied extensively for the adsorption of dyes. One study showed the crosslinking of chitosan (CS) with salicylaldehyde to prepare a hydrogel with enhanced surface porosity. The hydrogel showed remarkable adsorption performance with crystal violet (CV) and rose bengal (RB) dyes with approximately 98% (6.85 mg/g) and 99% (15.26 mg/g) removal, respectively. pH played a dominant role as the best adsorption capacity was achieved in pH 6 for CV, whereas it showed pH 3 for RB dyes. Mechanistic aspects revealed that Freundlich adsorption isotherm showed multilayer coverage over a heterogeneous surface, and kinetic studies

supported the pseudo-second-order model. The hydrogel also demonstrated good reusability and, because it was mostly derived from natural sources, was a very cost-effective option for adsorbent ([Fig. 16.3A](#_bookmark4)) ([Parshi et al., 2019](#_bookmark55)). Another work showed the photopolymerization of poly(ethylene glycol) macromer and acrylamide (AAm) monomer in the pres-ence of CS was used to create semi-interpenetrating network (semi-IPN) hydrogel composites for dye adsorption inves-tigations ([Zhao et al., 2012](#_bookmark77)). This hydrogel was used for the adsorption of four different types of dyes, acid red 18 (AR), acid orange 7 (AO), methyl orange (MO), and basic violet 14 (BV) ([Fig. 16.3B](#_bookmark4)). Compared to cationic BV 14, the hydrogel demonstrated high anionic dye adsorption capability for AR 18(342.54 mg/g), followed by AO 7 (221.10 mg/g), and MO (185.24 mg/g). Alternatively, in another noteworthy work, CS was crosslinked using oxalic acid to prepare a hydrogel that was further used for the adsorptive removal of reactive red dye. The ionic crosslinking of CS with oxalate ions improved the percentage of dye removal as well as the chemical stability of the biosorbent, with a maximum of 90.6% (110.74 mg/g) dye removal at pH 4. In this situation, the adsorption isotherm model demon-strated the best fit with the Redlich—Peterson equation. Both oxalic acid and CS are natural biomolecules that showed enhanced structural properties and also proved to be eco-friendly and efficient adsorbents for dye removal ([Pe´rez-Caldero´n, Santos, & Zaritzky, 2020](#_bookmark60)). Another similar work depicted the role of phytic acid as a crosslinker and carboxymethyl-CS as the natural biopolymer to prepare efficient hydrogels by in situ polymerization method, which was subsequently used for the removal of methyl orange and congo red dye. For MO (13.62 mg/g) and CR (8.49 mg/g), hydrogel showed good adsorption capability. Not only this, recyclability studies depicted that the hydrogel demon-strated unaltered characteristics for five adsorption/desorption cycles, thereby making it employable as a highly efficient adsorbent for the removal of toxic dye applications ([Han et al., 2021](#_bookmark28)) ([Fig. 16.4A](#_bookmark5)). Cellulose is another common bio-polymer used for dye adsorption applications. In a particular study, cellulose hydrogel was fabricated using a chemical dissolution procedure, and the prepared hydrogel was used for the removal of direct blue 86 dye from aquatic environ-ments. The hydrogel fitted well with Langmuir isotherm and pseudo-second-order kinetic graph and also showed a good adsorption capacity of 53.76 mg/g. The scientists inferred electrostatic interactions, as the main cause of absorp-tion between the positively charged hydrogel matrix and the negatively charged anionic dye ([Shoaib, Ragab, El Sikaily,](#_bookmark68) [Yılmaz, & El Nemr, 2023](#_bookmark68)). Another relevant study demonstrated the technique of direct radiation copolymerization to prepare carboxymethyl cellulose-_g_\-methacrylic acid/acrylamide poly(CMC/MAAc: AAm) hydrogel. After tuning the properties of the hydrogel by adjusting methacrylic acid and acrylamide content, an optimum hydrogel is prepared with good swelling behavior and then targeted toward cationic acid blue and anionic methyl green dye removal. Due to the presence of several free carboxylic acid groups, the hydrogel showed the tendency to form salts with methyl green cat-ionic dye, thereby depicting better affinity toward basic dye and good adsorptive removal ([El-Arnaouty, Abdel Ghaffar,](#_bookmark21) [Abdel Baky, & Shama, 2019](#_bookmark21)). In another piece of interesting work, nanocellulose was extracted from coconut husk fibers and incorporated inside CS biopolymer to prepare hydrogel beads. The adsorption performance of these beads

was investigated with CV and methylene blue (MB) dye removal. In the case of CV, 94.75%, and for MB, 95.88%, removal was achieved in 1 hour. The Freundlich model for MB adsorption and the Freundlich and Langmuir models for CV adsorption were found to provide the best representation of the isotherm data. Pseudo-second-order kinetic model for both dyes proved to be a well-correlated fit, indicating that chemisorption impacted the adsorption of MB and CV dyes onto the prepared hydrogel beads. The best feature of the hydrogels was that they maintained more than 60% adsorption efficiency even after seven adsorption—desorption cycles proving them to be a highly effective bioadsorbent for the removal of textile dyes ([Poornachandhra et al., 2023](#_bookmark61)).

A similar work showcased the use of a cellulose-based hydrogel crosslinked with ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid (EDTA) with a remarkable 92% crosslinking degree. The hydrogel demonstrated a remarkable adsorption uptake capac-ity of up to 2000 mg/g for MB cationic dye ([Jabir et al., 2022](#_bookmark34)). The results revealed noncovalent molecular adsor-bent—adsorbate interactions guided by molecular simulation studies.

Over the past few decades, research on guar gum and its derivatives has shown how very promising they are for use in a variety of sectors. Guar gum is the ground endosperm of _Cyamopsis tetragonoloba_ seeds, which are rich in galacto-mannan, a complex polymer. This high molecular weight polymer, rich in hydroxyl groups, is made up of a D-mannose backbone with side chains of D-galactose units connected. By forming hydrogen bonds with water, these functional groups give the solution viscosity and thickness, and on crosslinking and modification, they can be used to prepare bio-polymeric hydrogels with tremendous potential in wastewater treatment. Guar gum hydrogels were prepared using borax as a crosslinking agent and used for the decolorization of aniline blue dye. The hydrogels exhibited excellent adsorption characteristics with up to 94% removal in 60 minutes ([Thombare, Jha, Mishra, & Siddiqui, 2017](#_bookmark70)), whereas in another work, guar gum and acrylic acid (AA) were used using free-radical polymerization technique to prepare a hydrogel that showed a 93.8% removal of MB dye ([Sharma et al., 2015](#_bookmark64)). Another noteworthy work demonstrated the preparation of an interpenetrating network made from guar gum and polyacrylamide by polymerization and crosslink-ing. The gel was deemed fit for the adsorption of cationic dyes such as azure B and CV. It is noticed that both dyes CV and AB have an absorption efficiency of greater than 85%. Electrostatic interaction between the oppositely charged dye molecules and the gel system is observed to be the root cause of the dye absorption ([Hiremath and Vishalakshi, 2015](#_bookmark30)). In similar lines, xanthan gum is a high molar mass polysaccharide manufactured commercially through the aerobic fer-mentation of carbohydrates by the Gram-negative bacterium _Xanthomonas campestris_, with the addition of organic nitrogen sources and trace elements. Structurally, it is composed of trisaccharide branches consisting of D-glucuronic acid (β-1,2), D-mannose (β-1,4), and α-1,3 linkages connecting the cellulose backbone to the D-mannose. They also have several thickening properties that make them versatile and used in several dye decontamination industries. A group of researchers modified the xanthan gum by esterification process, followed by crosslinking using click chemistry to produce highly capable hydrogel adsorbents targeted at the removal of gentian violet dye with a superior adsorption capacity of 502 mg/g. The primary cause of the dye removal mechanism was identified as the electrostatic interactions

between the cationic dye and the polyanionic hydrogel, as well as the swelling properties of the hydrogel. The most striking feature of the hydrogel was its ability to maintain 99% removal capacity even after four consecutive cycles of adsorption and desorption ([Njuguna and Scho¨nherr, 2021](#_bookmark51)).

Sodium alginate, a linear polysaccharide that is a naturally occurring, water-soluble salt of alginic acid, commonly extracted from brown algae, is another source of biopolymer. It is easily extracted and has a high bioavailability. The α-L-guluronic and β-D-mannuronic acid residues that make up this natural polymer result in a range of consecutive 1,4-linkages with other neighboring chemical structures. Sodium alginate possesses the capacity to prepare hydrogels pri-marily due to the replacement of various divalent cations such as calcium, barium, and strontium for sodium ions that would otherwise be present in the guluronic acid residues ([Asadi, Eris, & Azizian, 2018](#_bookmark11)). Using calcium as a crosslin-ker, one work showcased the use of calcium alginate hydrogel beads that were further used for the removal of methyl violet dye, with a high adsorption capacity of 713 mg/g. In a similar study, gamma irradiation was used to create a sodium—alginate/acrylamide (Na—alginate/AAm) crosslinked hydrogel, which showed interesting adsorption results for the removal of basic violet dye, with an optimum adsorption capacity of 78.1 mg/g at pH 9 ([Gad, Aly, & Abdel-Aal,](#_bookmark22) [2011](#_bookmark22)). Recently, a work demonstrated the role of a potent hydrogel from sodium alginate (SA) that had been integrated with polyethyleneimine (PEI). The hydrogel was capable of removing 99% of MB dye from water with 0.5 g/L SA/PEI hydrogel at 100 mg/L starting concentration in roughly 30 minutes. The maximum MB adsorption capacity of the SA/ PEI hydrogel was 400.0 mg/g. Moreover, even after four consecutive adsorption—desorption cycles, the hydrogel remained effective with 60% adsorption capacity. Researchers believed that the amine groups introduced to the hydro-gel matrix by PEI molecules played acute binding sites for the adsorption of dye molecules following the chelation mechanism, thereby confirming its role as a highly cost-effective adsorbent for water decontamination ([Godiya, Xiao,](#_bookmark25) [& Lu, 2020](#_bookmark25)) ([Fig. 16.4B](#_bookmark5)). These natural biopolymers are excellent examples of how hydrogels can be prepared and used as eco-friendly and highly economical adsorbents for dye removal and water decontamination applications.

# Biopolymer hydrogel composites for dye removal

Hydrogels even though have emerged as one of the most superior adsorbent materials for dye removal, they also suffer certain drawbacks in terms of their mechanical rigidity, adsorption capacity as well as optimum regeneration abilities. Therefore scientists further delved deep into research to add certain other inorganic as well as organic materials, within the hydrogel matrix—such as metals, clays, carbon-based materials like graphene and carbon nanotubes, metallic nano-particles, biochar, and zeolites. MOFs and organic fillers—create composite materials with superior and enhanced mechanical, and chemical resistance, thermal stability, and adsorption capacity properties. The inherent features of the fillers, such as high surface area, abundant functional groups, and nonreactivity with the hydrogel matrix, can aid it, making it suitable for even promising results in dye adsorption. In comparison with pristine hydrogel polymers, com-posite hydrogels show better regeneration efficiency, more surface area, and hence greater adsorptive activity. An excel-lent illustration of this is the study on the adsorption of methylene blue (MB) dye using a hydrogel nanocomposite of gum ghatti grafted with polyacrylamide and TiO2 nanoparticles. Pure gum ghatti hydrogel showed an adsorption capac-ity of 555.55 mg/g, and polyacrylamide-grafted gum ghatti hydrogel showed an adsorption capacity of 769.23 mg/g toward MB dye. However, after incorporation of TiO2 nanoparticles, the adsorption capacity increased to a magnificent 1305.48 mg/g. Strong electrostatic interactions between the positively charged cationic dye molecules and the nega-tively charged adsorption active sites are the primary reason for adsorption efficacy ([Mittal and Ray, 2016](#_bookmark46)).

Graphene oxide derived from coal has several remarkable properties like different surface functional groups such as hydroxyl and carboxylic groups that show their potential in adsorption applications. A group of researchers prepared graphene oxide crosslinked nanocomposite hydrogels with CS and CMC polymers and checked for its application toward the removal of both cationic (MB) and anionic (methyl orange) dyes. About 99% (655.98 mg/g adsorption capacity for MB) and 82% (404.52 mg/g adsorption capacity for MO) were achieved. Not only this, the nanocomposite hydrogel showed astounding regeneration properties for continuous 20 adsorption—desorption cycles that only prove their versatility and extremely superior efficacy in wastewater treatment ([Mittal, Al Alili, Morajkar, & Alhassan, 2021](#_bookmark49)). Silver nanoparticles prepared particularly using green synthesis routes when incorporated inside a porous hydrogel matrix can result in nanocomposite hydrogel networks for superior dye removal applications. The microwave-assisted polymerization of acrylamide and 2-acrylamido-2-methyl-1-propanesulfonic acid (AMPS) in pectin solution containing sil-ver nanoparticles led to the preparation of a nanocomposite hydrogel that was used for the removal of crystal violet (CV) dye. An impressive 1950 mg/g adsorption capacity was achieved, which is very impressive in comparison to other reported literature. Overall, 97% CV could be even desorbed from the solution at acidic pH ([Kodoth and Badalamoole,](#_bookmark40) [2020](#_bookmark40)). Using a green hydrothermal technique, a unique self-assembled reduced graphene oxide hydrogel modified with

silver nanoparticles (AgNPs) and different porphyrin complexes was prepared and reported by another group of research-ers. This composite hydrogel showed a good adsorption capacity of up to 130.37 mg/g toward MB dye. As AgNPs and porphyrin complexes were included, the number of adsorption sites in the modified hydrogels multiplied, increasing their adsorption capacity ([Lim Teik Zheng, Phromsatit, Boonyuen, & Andou, 2020](#_bookmark44)). Another group reported the loading of magnetic graphene oxide nanoparticles inside CS biopolymer hydrogel using isophthaloyl chloride. Robust, mechanically strong, and surface-modified hydrogel beads were formed and used for the adsorption of both cationic and anionic dyes. The maximum adsorption capacities of cationic MB and anionic Eriochrome black T (EBT) were observed to be 289 and 292 mg/g, respectively. The incorporation of magnetic nanoparticles within the biopolymer matrix is reported to reduce the required dosage of the adsorbent, as well as improve surface area and separation speed. The Dubinin—Radushkevich model was used to fit isotherm data, which revealed that the adsorption mechanism was the result of physiosorption. The adsorption process was favorable, endothermic, and spontaneous, according to the thermodynamic data ([Jamali and](#_bookmark35) [Akbari, 2021](#_bookmark35)) ([Fig. 16.5](#_bookmark6)). Graphite was also utilized in the modification of sodium alginate biopolymer and graft polymer-ization of AA to prepare a porous hydrogel used for the adsorptive removal of malachite green dye. Under the most opti-mized experimental conditions, an adsorptive capacity of 628.93 mg/g was achieved, which is a remarkable feat. The authors believed electrostatic attraction and hydrogen bonding as the main reasons for enhanced adsorption efficacy. The predominant feature in this case was that the hydrogel demonstrated 91% removal of dye even after three consecutive adsorption—desorption cycles. Moreover, because graphite powder was utilized as a filler and sodium alginate served as the structural support, the prepared hydrogel composite is inexpensive, biodegradable, and environmentally benign making it an excellent choice for dye removal applications ([Verma et al., 2020](#_bookmark71)).

With its enormous surface area, layered structure, and strong cationic exchange capacity, montmorillonite clay is currently 20 times less expensive on the market than activated carbon. Through in situ polymerization, clay could also contribute to the creation of polymeric hydrogels with superior mechanical and optical transparency. Hence, in a study, using an aqueous solution of NaOH and urea, cellulose, CMC, and intercalated clay was chemically crosslinked to cre-ate superabsorbent hydrogels. For MB solutions at concentrations of 10 and 100 mg/L, the maximum removal efficien-cies of the hydrogel samples were 96.6% and 98%, respectively. The adsorption mechanism followed monolayer, spontaneous, physisorption, thereby depicting the promising role of clay-based hybrid hydrogels for dye decontamina-tion ([Peng et al., 2016](#_bookmark58)) ([Fig. 16.6](#_bookmark7)). Another group of researchers demonstrated the role of using ultrasound-assisted in

situ emulsion polymerization technique to create the poly(acrylamide)-kaolin (PAAm-K) hydrogel nanocomposite. They revealed that the use of kaolin as a crosslinking agent and ultrasound treatment in the synthesis process aided in the homogeneous dispersion of kaolin in the hydrogel matrix, boosting the hydrogel’s strength and durability and enhancing its ability to adsorb organic pollutants. The nanocomposite hydrogel was further utilized for the removal of CV dye and showed a decent adsorption capacity of 13.4 mg/g for an initial 30 mg dye concentration ([Shirsath, Patil,](#_bookmark67) [Bhanvase, & Sonawane, 2015](#_bookmark67)). The same group of researchers had previously conducted a study of the removal of bril-liant green dye by using polyacrylic acid—kaolin hydrogel composite (PAA-K) hydrogel that had shown 12.8 mg/g dye removal for the same initial concentration of dye. The polyacrylamide, therefore, enhanced the adsorption efficiency marginally. An important attribute to note here is that the synergistic combination of hydrogel adsorption and ultra-sound treatment played a key role in reducing the adsorption time from 5 hours to 30 minutes. Overall, 80% of dye removal was observed when the PAAm-K hydrogel was employed alone for experimental analysis, compared to 89% when both hydrogel and ultrasound were combined ([Shirsath et al., 2013](#_bookmark66)).

Zeolites are a broad class of hydrated aluminosilicates that are crystalline and porous and can hold water molecules, positively charged atomic groups, and even smaller organic molecules. They have a complex, three-dimensional struc-ture and have been reported to be used in several adsorption applications. Practically, they tend to coagulate and fre-quently aggregate in several working conditions. Hydrogels, although widely used as low-cost adsorbents, sometimes can be mechanically weak and tend to shear. A group of scientists tried to overcome both of their limitations by prepar-ing a composite hydrogel from polymethacrylic acid and two kinds of synthetic zeolites, namely hydrophilic zeolite A and hydrophobic zeolite ZSM-5. The composite hydrogel was thus utilized for the adsorptive removal of a cationic dye basic yellow 28 dye. The hydrogel composite was able to remove the dye with an adsorption capacity of 180 mg/g. Also, the scientists inferred that hydrogel composition, solution pH, dye composition, mass, and temperature played the defining role, and the type of zeolite had little significance in the adsorption efficacy. They defined the mechanism to be mostly physisorption, spontaneous, and also highlighted that the adsorption processes under investigation were well analyzed through the use of image analysis, which demonstrated a considerable effect of initial dye concentration on coloration uniformity and a linear link between equilibrium adsorption capabilities and coloration intensity ([Panic and](#_bookmark54) [Velickovic, 2014](#_bookmark54)). Another paper reported the viability of using gum karaya (GK) zeolite-Y integrated hydrogel com-posite (ZHC) as a possible adsorbent to remediate wastewater contaminated with cationic dyes. First, the crosslinked hydrogel of GK was prepared by grafting _N_\-isopropylacrylamide and AA, and then the zeolite-Y particles were evenly distributed throughout the polymer matrix. Brilliant green dye was used in dye adsorption studies, and an amazing adsorption capacity of 1461.35 mg/g was obtained. The maximum adsorption capacity of the native hydrogel was

836.19 mg/g, while native zeolite-Y showed maximum adsorption of 409.0 mg/g, which is less than the prepared com-posite hydrogel (1461.35 mg/g). This states the fact that the addition of zeolite, aided in the addition of more vacant adsorption sites that resulted in a better adsorptive performance of the compound hydrogel. While the dye molecules’ diffusion process followed both intraparticle and liquid film diffusion mechanisms, the adsorption kinetics followed a

pseudo-second-order kinetics equation. Additionally, the composite hydrogel demonstrated a removal effectiveness of 95% after six cycles of adsorption—desorption and was successfully regenerated using acetone following dye adsorption ([Mittal, Babu, Dabbawala, Stephen, & Alhassan, 2020](#_bookmark48)). These promising features make zeolite-integrated hydrogel composites a smart and effective choice for dye decontamination with excellent adsorption efficacy ([Klein et al., 2020;](#_bookmark39) [Ribeiro et al., 2019](#_bookmark39)).

In present times, biochar has emerged as a great adsorbent choice by researchers worldwide as it can easily be obtained from waste carbon-rich biomass (agricultural, poultry, sludge waste, etc.). They are mostly thermochemically improved by-products that have been prepared in limited oxygen supply ([Sachan and Das, 2022](#_bookmark62)). Alginate-kelp biochar hydrogel beads were prepared using Ca21 ions via physical crosslinking method, and its applicability as a composite hydrogel was tested with CV dye. The native hydrogel beads (Alg-B) showed an adsorption capacity of 3852.59 mg/g, whereas the biochar-loaded Alg-KBC1 showed an impressive 4545.70 mg/g removal. Increasing kelp biochar content, however, led to a decrease in the adsorption capacity that can be attributed to the blockage of active sites, resulting in the decrease of available surface area. The results indicated that both physisorption and chemisorption contributed to the adsorption process. Instead of the limitation of powdered biochar adsorbents, incorporating them in hydrogel matri-ces can prove to be an advantageous technique for dye removal applications ([Ohemeng-Boahen, Sewu, & Woo, 2019](#_bookmark53)). The different functional groups in the biochar can prepare covalent linkages with the hydrogel matrix to prepare an innovative, highly efficient hydrogel. Based on this knowledge, the biochar composite hydrogels were made in a single pot using xanthan gum as a macromolecular additive, AA, and 2-acrylamide-2-methylpropanesulfonic acid as mono-mers, rice and corn straw biochar as modifiers, ammonium persulfate as an initiator, _N,N_r\-methylene bisacrylamide as a crosslinking agent, and sodium lauryl sulfate as a porogen. At a pH of 6, the maximal removal efficiencies of corn bio-char and rice biochar hydrogel for MB dye are 81.58% and 94.71%, respectively, after 90 minutes. Researchers believe that π—π stacking, hydrogen bonding, pore diffusion, and electrostatic interactions are some of the reasons behind the mechanistic insights for dye adsorption ([Wang et al., 2022](#_bookmark73)). # Conclusion and future perspectives

As industries and technologies advance quickly and living standards grow in tandem, water contamination has become a major issue. Efficient, methodical, and critical methodologies are needed to create affordable, recyclable, biodegrad-able, and biocompatible adsorbents with high harmful pollutant removal efficiency from wastewater. Therefore, for effective wastewater treatment, researchers in both industrial and academic domains have become enthralled with the applications of smart biopolymer-based hydrogels. Hydrogels are insoluble, hydrophilic, and crosslinked polymers with a high swelling capacity that allows them to absorb a lot of water into their three-dimensional reticulated networks. Hydrogels made from biopolymers are highly regarded because of their readily available nature, biodegradability, biocompatibility, and environmental friendliness. One of the most popular and less expensive methods for removing contaminants from wastewater is adsorption on these biopolymers and hydrogels. The approach’s economic significance and commercial viability stem from the recycling of adsorbents and the low likelihood of hazardous leftovers. However, they have some limitations when it comes to practical applications. Mechanically, they are not strong and tough in some cases for proper reusability. In this regard, researchers have delved into the combination of hydrogels with other materials that can enhance the adsorption efficacy as well as stabilize the hydrogel network by modification. Excellent dye absorption capacity has been demonstrated by many novel functional hydrogels, with maximal absorption and selectivity for porous materials. This chapter has highlighted some of the noteworthy works on different kinds of biopolymeric hydrogels, alone and in combination with other materials such as graphene oxides, MOFs, zeolites, bio-char, and nanoparticles for enhanced adsorption of a number of cationic and anionic dyes. The influence of pH, along with inherent electrostatic interactions, H-bonding, π—π stacking, and pore diffusion between the adsorbent and the adsorbate play one of the most dominating roles for dye adsorption. These hydrogels can be easily regenerated and

reutilized up to several cycles making the process highly economical and feasible. However, it is necessary to investi-gate and evaluate the viability of using such engineered hydrogels in drinking water, municipal, and industrial treatment systems. Overall, the use of biopolymer-based natural materials for the preparation of hydrogel is a cost-effective, yet lucrative approach for not only dyes but many other contaminants from wastewater, thereby expanding new horizons in dye removal technologies. Thorough investigation and research ought to concentrate on the practical uses of engineered biopolymeric hydrogels so that their large-scale manufacturing and economic feasibility can be assessed.
